receptors.therapeuticEffect: Anxiolytic, antidepressant, reduces EPS
receptors.sideEffects: Dizziness, nausea (usually mild)

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Modulates serotonin release at terminals; implicated in depression, OCD, migraine. Vortioxetine agonist target.
receptors.sideEffects: Generally well tolerated; dizziness possible

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Modulates serotonin and glutamate release presynaptically; vortioxetine antagonist target contributing to pro-cognitive profile.
receptors.sideEffects: Generally well tolerated

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Reduces EPS risk, improves negative symptoms, antidepressant
receptors.sideEffects: Sedation, weight gain (mild)

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Increases DA & NE release in PFC
receptors.sideEffects: Weight gain, increased appetite

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Pro-cognitive, anti-emetic
receptors.sideEffects: Constipation (rare)

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Disinhibits glutamate and acetylcholine release in frontal cortex — pro-cognitive, memory enhancement.
receptors.sideEffects: Generally well tolerated

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Pro-cognitive, circadian regulation
receptors.sideEffects: Usually well tolerated

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Increases synaptic serotonin
receptors.sideEffects: Nausea, sexual dysfunction, GI upset, insomnia, headache

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Increases synaptic norepinephrine
receptors.sideEffects: Hypertension, tachycardia, sweating, tremor, urinary retention

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Increases synaptic dopamine
receptors.sideEffects: Insomnia, agitation, psychosis risk, appetite suppression

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Prefrontal cortex activation; working memory; synergistic with D2 in striatum; D1 stimulation — cognitive enhancement.
receptors.sideEffects: Dyskinesias (excess agonism); cognitive blunting (antagonism at therapeutic doses generally mild)

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Antipsychotic action at 60–70% occupancy; antiemetic
receptors.sideEffects: EPS, hyperprolactinemia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Negative symptom improvement; cognitive enhancement; reward circuit modulation; reduced craving. Highest clinical relevance for cariprazine.
receptors.sideEffects: Similar to D2 but generally milder EPS risk; akathisia possible

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Prefrontal cortex modulation; implicated in clozapine's atypical antipsychotic profile and low EPS despite antipsychotic efficacy.
receptors.sideEffects: Generally well tolerated at clinical doses

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Sedation, anxiolytic
receptors.sideEffects: Sedation, weight gain, cognitive dulling

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Reduces EPS (offsets D2 blockade)
receptors.sideEffects: Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, cognitive impairment

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Sedation, anxiolytic
receptors.sideEffects: Orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, reflex tachycardia, nasal congestion

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Increases NE & 5-HT release
receptors.sideEffects: Sedation (paradoxical), weight gain

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Anxiolytic, sedative, anticonvulsant, muscle relaxant
receptors.sideEffects: Sedation, dependence, respiratory depression, cognitive impairment

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Inhibition increases 5-HT, NE, and DA in synaptic cleft — antidepressant. MAO-A preferentially degrades 5-HT and NE.
receptors.sideEffects: Hypertensive crisis with tyramine (cheese reaction), serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs, dietary restrictions mandatory

receptors.action: Irreversible inhibition (at low doses: selective; at high doses: non-selective)
receptors.therapeuticEffect: MAO-B preferentially degrades dopamine and phenylethylamine. Selective MAO-B inhibition — increased dopamine (antiparkinsonian, adjunct antidepressant at high doses). Low dietary restriction risk at selective doses.
receptors.sideEffects: At non-selective doses: same tyramine risk as MAO-A inhibition; insomnia, agitation

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Inhibition prevents acetylcholine breakdown — increases synaptic ACh in cortex and hippocampus — pro-cognitive, symptomatic treatment of dementia.
receptors.sideEffects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea (GI cholinergic), bradycardia, nightmares, muscle cramps, urinary urgency

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Rapid antidepressant action (ketamine/esketamine via AMPA potentiation); antidementia (memantine — low-affinity antagonist reduces excitotoxicity); dissociative anesthesia.
receptors.sideEffects: Dissociation, psychotomimetic effects, hemodynamic stimulation, cognitive impairment, abuse potential

receptors.therapeuticEffect: MT1: circadian rhythm regulation, sleep promotion via SCN inhibition. MT2: sleep phase shifting, circadian resynchronization. Combined activation — antidepressant effect (agomelatine mechanism).
receptors.sideEffects: Generally well tolerated; hepatotoxicity specific to agomelatine (requires LFT monitoring)

receptors.therapeuticEffect: Neuroprotection, neuroplasticity, modulation of NMDA and other ion channels; possible cognitive and antidepressant benefit. Fluvoxamine is the only SSRI with significant Sigma-1 activity.
receptors.sideEffects: Generally well tolerated

drugs.name: Fluoxetine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Longest t½ of SSRIs — least withdrawal risk. Activating profile. Most studied SSRI in pregnancy. Wait 5 weeks before MAOI. FDA-approved for children (>7yo for OCD, >8yo for MDD).
drugs.pregnancy: Relatively well-studied; generally considered when benefits outweigh risks
drugs.metabolism: CYP2D6 substrate & potent inhibitor; CYP2C9 inhibitor

drugs.name: Sertraline
drugs.clinicalPearls: Most FDA indications of any SSRI. Mild DAT inhibition. Fewer CYP interactions than fluoxetine/paroxetine. Often first-line in cardiac patients. Preferred in breastfeeding.
drugs.pregnancy: Often considered first-line SSRI in pregnancy

drugs.name: Paroxetine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Most anticholinergic & sedating SSRI. Worst discontinuation syndrome (short t½, no active metabolites). Potent CYP2D6 inhibitor — watch for interactions. Non-linear kinetics.

drugs.name: Citalopram
drugs.clinicalPearls: Max dose 40 mg/day (20 mg in elderly, hepatic impairment, CYP2C19 poor metabolizers) due to QTc prolongation. Fewest CYP interactions among SSRIs. R-enantiomer may limit efficacy.

drugs.name: Escitalopram
drugs.clinicalPearls: S-enantiomer of citalopram — more potent, cleaner binding. Most selective SSRI. Often best tolerated. Max 20 mg. Considered first-line for many anxiety and depressive disorders.
drugs.pregnancy: Generally acceptable when benefits outweigh risks

drugs.name: Fluvoxamine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Only SSRI not FDA-approved for MDD. Potent CYP1A2 inhibitor (raises clozapine, theophylline, caffeine levels). Sigma-1 receptor agonist — possible cognitive benefit. BID dosing above 100 mg.

drugs.name: Venlafaxine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Dose-dependent pharmacology: <150 mg mostly serotonergic, >150 mg adds NE, >300 mg weak DA. Monitor BP above 150 mg. More toxic than SSRIs in overdose. Short t½ — bad withdrawal. Active metabolite = desvenlafaxine.
drugs.pregnancy: Third trimester use associated with neonatal adaptation syndrome
drugs.metabolism: CYP2D6 substrate (to active metabolite); minimal CYP inhibition

drugs.name: Desvenlafaxine
sideEffects: Similar to venlafaxine but potentially better tolerated
drugs.clinicalPearls: Active metabolite of venlafaxine. More consistent NE activity across doses. Less CYP interactions. Fixed dose (50 mg usually sufficient). Cannot be split/crushed.
drugs.metabolism: Primarily renal & UGT metabolism; minimal CYP involvement

drugs.name: Duloxetine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Strong pain indication profile — useful for depression + pain comorbidity. AVOID in hepatic impairment & heavy alcohol use. Cannot be split/crushed. 5× more 5-HT than NE potency. Moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor.

drugs.name: Levomilnacipran
drugs.clinicalPearls: Most noradrenergic SNRI (2× NE > 5-HT selectivity). More activating. Useful for fatigue-predominant depression. Watch for urinary retention esp. in BPH. Dose adjust in renal impairment.
drugs.metabolism: CYP3A4 substrate; no significant CYP inhibition

drugs.name: Bupropion
drugs.clinicalPearls: NO sexual dysfunction, NO weight gain (may cause weight loss). NDRI mechanism. Seizure risk increases above 450 mg — CONTRAINDICATED in eating disorders, seizure hx, abrupt alcohol/benzo withdrawal. Good augmentation to SSRIs. Dopaminergic — activating profile.

drugs.name: Mirtazapine
drugs.clinicalPearls: NaSSA mechanism — alpha-2 antagonism increases NE & 5-HT release. More sedating at LOWER doses (15 mg = mainly H1; higher doses add noradrenergic activation). No sexual dysfunction. No nausea (5-HT3 blockade). Good for underweight/insomniac depressed patients. "California rocket fuel" = venlafaxine + mirtazapine.

drugs.name: Trazodone

dosing.start: 50 mg at bedtime (for sleep); 150 mg/day for depression
dosing.frequency: Once daily at bedtime or divided

drugs.clinicalPearls: SARI (5-HT2A antagonist/reuptake inhibitor). Primarily used for insomnia at low doses, NOT as antidepressant (requires higher doses). Priapism risk — counsel male patients. mCPP active metabolite (anxiogenic). Relatively safe in overdose.
drugs.pregnancy: Limited data but generally considered acceptable for insomnia

drugs.name: Vortioxetine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Multimodal: SERT inhibition + 5-HT1A agonism + 5-HT3/7 antagonism. Pro-cognitive effects (unique among antidepressants). Reduce dose by 50% in CYP2D6 poor metabolizers. Very long t½ but still daily dosing. Less sexual dysfunction than SSRIs.
drugs.metabolism: CYP2D6 substrate; no significant CYP inhibition

drugs.name: Vilazodone
drugs.clinicalPearls: SPARI (SSRI + 5-HT1A partial agonist). MUST take with food (doubles absorption). Less sexual dysfunction than SSRIs. Slow titration required.
drugs.metabolism: CYP3A4 substrate; no significant CYP inhibition

drugs.name: Agomelatine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Melatonin receptor agonist (MT1/MT2) + 5-HT2C antagonist. Unique mechanism — circadian rhythm resynchronization. No sexual dysfunction, no weight gain. MANDATORY liver function monitoring. Not available in US. Dose at 9 PM.
drugs.metabolism: CYP1A2 (90%), CYP2C9; avoid with CYP1A2 inhibitors

drugs.name: Amitriptyline
drugs.clinicalPearls: Tertiary amine TCA — more serotonergic, more side effects. Metabolized to nortriptyline (active). Very dangerous in overdose (lethal dose ~10× therapeutic). ECG before starting. Now mainly used for pain/migraine at low doses.
drugs.pregnancy: Most data among TCAs; nortriptyline preferred

drugs.name: Nortriptyline
drugs.clinicalPearls: Secondary amine TCA — more noradrenergic, better tolerated. Therapeutic window: 50–150 ng/mL (levels useful). Best-studied TCA for therapeutic drug monitoring. Preferred TCA in elderly. Active metabolite of amitriptyline.

drugs.name: Clomipramine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Gold standard for OCD (most serotonergic TCA). Max 250 mg/day to reduce seizure risk. Metabolized to desmethylclomipramine (noradrenergic). Useful when SSRIs fail in OCD. Levels monitoring available.
drugs.pregnancy: Limited data; risks of TCAs apply

drugs.name: Phenelzine
drugs.halfLife: Short plasma t½; irreversible effect ~2 weeks
drugs.clinicalPearls: Irreversible, non-selective MAOI. Highly effective for atypical depression (hypersomnia, hyperphagia, rejection sensitivity). STRICT dietary restrictions (tyramine). 14-day washout before/after serotonergic drugs (5 weeks after fluoxetine). Pyridoxine (B6) depletion. Weight gain common.

drugs.name: Tranylcypromine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Structurally related to amphetamine — more activating than phenelzine, less weight gain. Same dietary restrictions. Stimulant-like properties can help fatigue. Often tried when phenelzine causes too much weight gain.

drugs.name: Selegiline patch
sideEffects: At 6 mg: no dietary restrictions needed
drugs.clinicalPearls: ONLY transdermal MAOI. At 6 mg/24hr: NO dietary restrictions (bypasses GI MAO-A). At 9–12 mg/24hr: dietary restrictions apply. Still need 14-day washout with serotonergic drugs. Selective MAO-B at low doses, non-selective at higher doses.
drugs.metabolism: Transdermal: avoids first-pass GI MAO inhibition

drugs.name: Haloperidol
drugs.clinicalPearls: High-potency FGA — very selective D2 antagonist. Gold standard for acute psychosis/agitation. IV haloperidol prolongs QTc — ECG monitoring required. Available as decanoate (LAI q4 weeks). Low sedation, low anticholinergic but HIGH EPS. D2 occupancy ~80% at 4 mg.
drugs.pregnancy: Most data among antipsychotics; relatively well-studied

drugs.name: Chlorpromazine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Low-potency FGA — the original antipsychotic (1952). "Dirty drug" — hits many receptors. Low EPS but high sedation/autonomic effects. Photosensitivity & skin pigmentation changes unique to phenothiazines. Dose equivalency reference: 100 mg chlorpromazine = standard unit.

drugs.name: Fluphenazine
drugs.clinicalPearls: High-potency piperazine phenothiazine. Available as decanoate LAI (q2–4 weeks). Similar to haloperidol in receptor profile. One of oldest depot formulations.

drugs.name: Perphenazine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Mid-potency piperazine phenothiazine. CATIE trial: compared favorably to olanzapine in effectiveness. Less EPS than high-potency FGAs, less sedation than low-potency. Available as decanoate.

drugs.name: Trifluoperazine

dosing.range: 15–20 mg/day (up to 40 mg in resistant cases)

drugs.clinicalPearls: High-potency piperazine phenothiazine. Similar to haloperidol but more sedating. Less used now but historically significant. Useful for agitation when sedation is desirable.

drugs.name: Zuclopenthixol
drugs.halfLife: 20 hrs oral; acetate IM 2–3 days; decanoate ~3 weeks

dosing.range: Oral: 20–60 mg/day; Acetate IM: 50–150 mg q2–3d; Decanoate: 200–400 mg q2–4wk

drugs.clinicalPearls: Three formulations with very different durations: oral (daily), acetate IM (days — 'Acuphase', useful for acute agitation without committing to long-acting depot), decanoate (weeks). Not available in the US.

drugs.name: Risperidone
drugs.clinicalPearls: Potent D2 & 5-HT2A antagonist. Dose-dependent EPS (atypical <6 mg, typical-like >6 mg). Highest prolactin of all SGAs. Active metabolite = paliperidone. Available as Risperdal Consta LAI (q2 weeks). FDA-approved for autism irritability.
drugs.pregnancy: Some reassuring data; monitor for EPS in neonate

drugs.name: Paliperidone
drugs.clinicalPearls: Active metabolite of risperidone (9-hydroxyrisperidone). Minimal CYP metabolism — fewer drug interactions. Dose-adjust in renal impairment. Available as Invega Sustenna (monthly LAI) and Invega Trinza (q3 month LAI). Extended-release oral formulation.
drugs.metabolism: Minimal hepatic metabolism; primarily renal excretion

drugs.name: Olanzapine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Pharmacologically similar to clozapine but without agranulocytosis risk. HIGHEST metabolic risk (with clozapine). Smoking decreases levels (CYP1A2 induction). Effective for acute agitation (IM). Olanzapine + fluoxetine (Symbyax) for bipolar depression/TRD. Lybalvi = olanzapine + samidorphan (opioid antagonist to mitigate weight gain).

drugs.name: Quetiapine

dosing.range: Schizophrenia: 300–800 mg; Bipolar: 300–800 mg; Depression: 150–300 mg

drugs.clinicalPearls: Very low D2 affinity — lowest EPS and prolactin of SGAs. Highly sedating (H1). Active metabolite norquetiapine has NET inhibition (antidepressant effect). Only SGA with 3 mood indications (mania, bipolar depression, MDD augmentation). Widely prescribed off-label for insomnia (controversial). XR formulation allows once-daily dosing.

drugs.name: Clozapine
drugs.clinicalPearls: ONLY antipsychotic proven superior in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Only drug (besides lithium) to reduce suicidality. Requires REMS/ANC monitoring. Therapeutic level: 350–500 mcg/L. Smoking reduces levels (CYP1A2). Fluvoxamine raises levels. Sialorrhea is paradoxical (M4 agonism). Lowest D2 affinity of all antipsychotics. Avoid abrupt discontinuation (cholinergic rebound).
drugs.pregnancy: Use only if clearly needed; limited data

drugs.name: Aripiprazole
drugs.clinicalPearls: D2 PARTIAL AGONIST (3rd generation) — stabilizes dopamine (reduces where high, increases where low). Minimal weight gain, minimal metabolic effects, no prolactin elevation, minimal sedation. Most activating SGA. Akathisia is dose-limiting. Available as Abilify Maintena LAI (monthly) and Aristada (q4–8 weeks). Very long t½.

drugs.name: Brexpiprazole
drugs.clinicalPearls: Similar to aripiprazole but with stronger 5-HT2A and Alpha-1 blockade — LESS akathisia, slightly more sedating. First FDA-approved drug for agitation in Alzheimer dementia. D2 partial agonist with more balanced receptor profile.

drugs.name: Cariprazine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Highest D3 affinity of any antipsychotic — may help negative symptoms and cognition. D3/D2 partial agonist. Very long effective half-life (2–3 weeks with metabolites) — effects persist weeks after discontinuation. Only SGA approved for bipolar depression (besides quetiapine, lurasidone, lumateperone, olanzapine-fluoxetine).

drugs.name: Lurasidone
drugs.clinicalPearls: Metabolically friendly — minimal weight gain & lipid effects. MUST take with food (350+ calories doubles absorption). Strong 5-HT7 antagonism (pro-cognitive). Approved for bipolar depression in adolescents. AVOID grapefruit juice. No significant QTc effect.

drugs.name: Ziprasidone
drugs.clinicalPearls: Most weight-neutral SGA (with aripiprazole). QTc prolongation concern — ECG at baseline & monitor. MUST take with food (doubles absorption). BID dosing required. Has SERT and NET inhibition (antidepressant-like properties). Short t½. IM form for acute agitation.

drugs.name: Lumateperone
drugs.clinicalPearls: Novel mechanism: potent 5-HT2A antagonist + moderate D2 presynaptic partial agonist + D1 modulation + SERT inhibition. Fixed dose (42 mg). Metabolically favorable. Low EPS risk. Newest indication for MDD adjunct (2023). Glutamate modulation via D1 receptor.

drugs.name: Amisulpride

dosing.start: Negative sx: 50 mg/day; Positive sx: 400 mg/day

sideEffects: Highest prolactin elevation of ALL antipsychotics
drugs.clinicalPearls: Highly selective D2/D3 antagonist — no histamine, muscarinic, or adrenergic binding. No weight gain, no sedation, no anticholinergic effects. Highest prolactin elevation of ALL antipsychotics. QTc prolongation. Dose-adjust in renal impairment. Not available in US — available across much of Europe.
drugs.pregnancy: Limited data; high prolactin may affect fertility
drugs.metabolism: Not CYP metabolized — primarily renal excretion

drugs.name: Asenapine
drugs.clinicalPearls: SUBLINGUAL ONLY — oral bioavailability is <2%, sublingual is ~35%. Do not eat/drink for 10 minutes after. Rich receptor binding profile (one of the broadest of all SGAs). Moderate weight gain. Available as transdermal patch.
drugs.metabolism: CYP1A2 substrate; UGT1A4; mild CYP2D6 inhibitor

drugs.name: Lithium
drugs.clinicalPearls: Gold standard mood stabilizer. ONLY drug proven to reduce suicide (with clozapine). Narrow therapeutic window. Monitor levels, renal function (Cr, eGFR), thyroid (TSH), calcium, ECG. Toxicity: >1.5 mEq/L. Dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides INCREASE levels. Toxicity triad: tremor, GI, mental status changes. NOT metabolized by liver. Pregnancy: Ebstein anomaly (lower risk than previously thought ~0.1%).
drugs.pregnancy: Ebstein anomaly risk; use only if clearly needed; fetal echo at 16–20 weeks

drugs.name: Valproate

dosing.start: Mania: 20–30 mg/kg/day loading; or 250–500 mg BID

drugs.clinicalPearls: Effective for acute mania (can load for rapid onset). Therapeutic level: 50–125 mcg/mL. Highly protein-bound (interactions). DOUBLES lamotrigine levels. HIGHLY TERATOGENIC — AVOID in women of childbearing potential (neural tube defects, cognitive impairment in offspring). Monitor LFTs, CBC, levels. Drug of choice for mixed episodes.
drugs.pregnancy: CONTRAINDICATED — highest teratogenicity of mood stabilizers
drugs.metabolism: CYP2C9, 2C19, UGT; inhibits CYP2C9, UGT (raises lamotrigine)

drugs.name: Lamotrigine
sideEffects: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / TEN (dose-dependent, slow titration mandatory)
drugs.clinicalPearls: Best evidence for bipolar DEPRESSION prevention. VERY slow titration (risk of SJS — 0.1% in adults, 1% in children). Valproate DOUBLES lamotrigine levels (halve dose). Carbamazepine HALVES lamotrigine levels. Estrogen-containing OCP decreases levels. Weight-neutral. No lab monitoring required. Na+ channel blockade mechanism.
drugs.pregnancy: Relatively favorable safety profile; dose may need adjustment
drugs.metabolism: UGT1A4 glucuronidation; NOT a CYP substrate

drugs.name: Carbamazepine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Potent enzyme INDUCER — lowers levels of many drugs (OCP, warfarin, other anticonvulsants, antipsychotics). Autoinduction — dose needs increase over first weeks. Therapeutic level: 4–12 mcg/mL. Test HLA-B*1502 before starting (SJS risk in Southeast Asian descent). Monitor CBC, Na+, LFTs. Na+ channel blockade mechanism.

drugs.name: Lorazepam
drugs.clinicalPearls: Intermediate-acting BZD. NO active metabolites — safe in hepatic impairment (with oxazepam, temazepam: "LOT" — Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam for liver disease). Available PO, IM, IV. Drug of choice for catatonia. IM absorption predictable (unlike diazepam IM).

drugs.name: Clonazepam
drugs.clinicalPearls: Long-acting, high-potency BZD. Smooth anxiolytic effect (long t½). Good for sustained anxiety control. Anticonvulsant properties. Useful for akathisia treatment. High potency = higher dependence potential. Equivalence: 0.5 mg clonazepam ≈ 10 mg diazepam.

drugs.name: Diazepam
drugs.clinicalPearls: Very long-acting BZD with active metabolites. Gold standard for alcohol withdrawal (long-acting, self-tapering). Rapid onset PO. Poor/erratic IM absorption. Multiple active metabolites accumulate in elderly — AVOID in geriatrics. Equivalence reference: 10 mg diazepam = standard BZD unit.
drugs.pregnancy: Category D; avoid in first trimester

drugs.name: Alprazolam
drugs.clinicalPearls: Short-to-intermediate t½. High-potency BZD — high dependence risk. Particularly problematic discontinuation (taper over weeks). Avoid in hepatic impairment. Equivalence: 0.5 mg alprazolam ≈ 10 mg diazepam.

drugs.name: Zolpidem
sideEffects: Complex sleep behaviors (sleepwalking, driving) — FDA black box
drugs.clinicalPearls: Alpha-1 selective — primarily hypnotic, less anxiolytic. Next-day impairment possible. Complex sleep behaviors (sleepwalking, driving) — FDA black box. Lower abuse potential than BZDs but still Schedule IV. Women metabolize more slowly — use 5 mg dose.

drugs.name: Zopiclone

dosing.start: Eszopiclone: 1 mg; Zopiclone: 3.75 mg at bedtime

drugs.clinicalPearls: Metallic/bitter taste common with zopiclone. Eszopiclone is the S-enantiomer. Approved for long-term use (unlike most hypnotics). Similar complex sleep behavior risk to zolpidem.

drugs.name: Buspirone
drugs.clinicalPearls: 5-HT1A partial agonist — NOT a benzodiazepine. No sedation, no dependence, no withdrawal. Takes 2–4 weeks for effect. Ineffective for acute anxiety/panic. Will NOT prevent BZD withdrawal. No abuse potential. May help SSRI augmentation and SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction.

drugs.name: Hydroxyzine

dosing.range: Anxiety: 50–100 mg QID; Insomnia: 50–100 mg at bedtime

drugs.clinicalPearls: Not a BZD — no dependence, no abuse potential. Good for anxiety in patients with substance use disorders. Sedating H1 antagonist. QTc prolongation at high doses. Active metabolite: cetirizine (Zyrtec).

drugs.name: Methylphenidate

dosing.frequency: Two to three times daily (IR) or once daily (ER)

drugs.clinicalPearls: Blocks DAT and NET — increases synaptic DA and NE. D-threo enantiomer is active. Multiple ER formulations differ in release profiles. Monitor growth, weight, CV parameters.
drugs.metabolism: Not significantly metabolized by CYP; de-esterified by plasma esterases

drugs.name: Lisdexamfetamine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Prodrug — abuse deterrent design. Only stimulant FDA-approved for BED. Long duration allows single morning dosing. Releases DA and NE into synapse (reversal of transporters) rather than just blocking reuptake.
drugs.metabolism: Cleaved by red blood cell esterases to d-amphetamine; minimal CYP involvement

drugs.name: Atomoxetine
drugs.clinicalPearls: NOT a stimulant — no abuse potential, not a controlled substance. Takes 4–6 weeks for full effect. Black box: suicidality risk in children/adolescents (like antidepressants). Useful in ADHD + anxiety or substance abuse comorbidity.
drugs.metabolism: CYP2D6 substrate; poor metabolizers have 5× higher exposure

drugs.name: Guanfacine ER
drugs.clinicalPearls: Selective alpha-2A agonist — tightens PFC 'signal-to-noise'. Not sedating like clonidine. No cardiac monitoring required routinely. Useful adjunct to stimulants or monotherapy when stimulants not tolerated.

drugs.name: Donepezil
indications: Mild, moderate, and severe Alzheimer dementia
drugs.clinicalPearls: Once-daily dosing (long t½). 5 mg for 4–6 weeks before increasing to 10 mg. 23 mg dose has marginal additional benefit over 10 mg with more GI side effects. Available as orally disintegrating tablet. GI side effects (nausea, diarrhea) are the main tolerability issue.

drugs.name: Rivastigmine
drugs.halfLife: ~1–2 hrs plasma; extended CNS effect via patch
drugs.clinicalPearls: Patch formulation dramatically reduces GI side effects (same efficacy). Drug of choice for Parkinson disease dementia. Titrate slowly to reduce cholinergic side effects. No CYP drug interactions.
drugs.metabolism: Not CYP metabolized — hydrolyzed by AChE itself

drugs.name: Galantamine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Unique nicotinic APL mechanism. Must be taken with food to reduce GI side effects. Available in ER formulation (once daily). Similar efficacy to other AChEIs.

drugs.name: Memantine
drugs.clinicalPearls: Complementary mechanism to AChEIs — often combined (Namzaric = memantine ER + donepezil). Different from ketamine: low-affinity binding avoids psychotomimetic effects. Dose-adjust in renal impairment. Generally well tolerated.
drugs.metabolism: Primarily renal excretion; not significantly CYP metabolized
